Prison: Punishment or Safe Haven?

By: Mart-Marie Faure | Production

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Why some female prisoners find prison a safe haven rather than punishment.

Unique Selling Point:
Some women look at prison as a safe haven, getting away from abusive relationships.escaping poverty and ensuring good care for their babies.

Summary:
There are approximately 4 174 women incarcerated in correctional facilities in South Africa one of the lowest percentages in the world.
Women mostly receive prison sentences for fraud and theft rather than violent crimes. In contrast to overpopulated and violent male prisons, the women's facility in Oudtshoorn is almost home to some. These women feel that they are better off in prison away from abusive partners, poverty, alcohol and drugs. Women with babies are kept in a facility adjacent to the prison. Babies are allowed to stay with their mothers until they are two years old. There are contradicting thoughts about children in prison which we will explore.

Further information:
South Africa has one of the lowest percentages of female prisoners in the world. Although not much research is available to explain why, the report into SA prisons think that the reason is that women are less aggressive, have fever chances to commit crime because of cultural reason. It may also be that the courts are more lenient when sentencing females to direct imprisonment.

Airfare, Accommodation and Car hire.

Script:


Prison – Safe Haven to women
SCRIPT
Wide shot: Prison exterior
Derek Link on camera
This small national heritage building in the middle of Oudtshoorn, is a prison for women

V/O
DEREK South Africa has one of the lowest percentages of female prisoners in the world. Currently there are approximately 4 174 women incarcerated in correctional facilities across the country.

This prison houses women sentenced for crimes ranging from theft to murder, and to some this is their safe haven.

DAWN JANTJIES
I stabbed my boyfriend.
DEREK: Is he alive?
No, he is dead.

ASENCIA MOOS

I am in prison for robbery, three years imprisonment, but I am back again. I got a second chance but I am back for breaking parole.


Ek is vir roof in die tronk, drie jaar gevangenis straf, maar ek is weer terug. Ek het ‘n tweede kans gekry, maar ek is weer terug vir parool breek.
V/O
DEREK Many of these women come from the poor surrounding townships where gang violence, drugs and abuse is rife.

V/O Asencia Moos was raised by her grandmother, Ouma Moos in Bridgtown, a township adjacent to Oudtshoorn.
OUMA MOOS
She went to school, she attended school regularly. Sy't skool gegaan en sy't gereeld in die skool gewees.
ASENCIA MOOS
When I became sexually active, everything changed. I left school and started smoking drugs.
Toe ek begin seksueel aktief raak het alles verander. Ek het die skool gelos en begin drugs rook.
V/O At the age of 20 Asencia was arrested for robbery and sentenced to three years in prison. After serving nine months, Asencia was released on parole but¬ quickly reverted to her old ways.
OUMA MOOS
They continue throughout the night.
They go and rob people. Then, at dawn they come back and sleep in the car behind the house.



Hulle loop mos nou dwarsdeur die nag. Loop en mense roof en steel en alles doen. Dan kom hulle teen voordag dan kom le hulle agter my huis in die kar.
V/O Overwelmed by life outside the safety of the prison walls. Asencia blatantly violated her parole conditions and one morning the authorities came knocking on Ouma Moos' door...
OUMA MOOS
When I went to call her. She got out of that car, She was so glad to see that officer, She said that she had been waiting a long time for them, that she wanted to go home. Toe ek haar nou gaan roep. Toe sy uit daai kar uitklim toe is sy so bly vir die bewaarder. Toe se sy sy wag al lankal vir hulle, sy wil terug gaan huistoe.
ASENCIA MOOS
I broke my parole conditions because I just felt that I didn’t want to be out there. Everything was just too much for me. Ek het my parool voorwaardes nie teegekom nie omdat ek het net gevoel ek wil nie meer daar buite wees nie want alles het vir my te veel geraak.
V/O Judge Johann vd Westhuizen is the Inspecting Judge for Correctional Services and through his investigations has first hand knowledge into the prisoners lives and the conditions that they live in.
JUDGE JOHANN vd WESTHUIZEN
INSPECTING JUDGE FOR CORRECTIONAL SERVICES (JICS) It is well known that some people prefer to come back when they go out on parole.
There may be several reasons, the first one is of course that while they are on parole their lives may not be all that easy. They depend on a caretaker, otherwise you can’t get parole .The caretaker might be a husband or a boyfriend or a family member who actually exploits the opportunity to abuse you or to use you for further crime.
So it is quite possible that they say it’s better for me inside than to be out on parole. What that says of our society of course is a different question.
V/O
DEREK Contrary to belief, correctional facilities are by no means luxurious, with many being highly over-crowded and depressing places. But as far as prisons go the one here in Oudtshoorn is almost an uplifting experience. Inmates are encouraged to learn skills and partake in various programmes designed to make eventual integration into society easier.

V/O Sharmaine Tya Tya, the Acting Manager for Legal Services at the Department of Correctional Services says their aim is to get prisoners to accept responsibility for themselves and their actions.
SHARMAINE TYA TYA
ACTING MANAGER: LEGAL SERVICES, SOUTHERN CAPE MANAGEMENT AREA.
Instead of saying we're trying to punish them, we're trying to help them, we're trying to bring back the self-confidence, the humanity in them. So that society out there can see that there's a person in this person. So we're trying to correct the wrong behaviour of outside by doing all the programmes and things that we have in prison.
DAWN JANTJIES They have anger management in and out. And there is a lot of the social workers' programmes like drugs and alcohol. And it is free to go also. There's a lot of stuff, but I finished that. And skills also.

Derek: What skills have you learnt? I see here in the kitchen you've learnt culinary skills.

No Sir there's lot of skills that you can do here in prison, like beads, needle work – everything like that.
V/O
DEREK South African law provides for children to remain in prison with their mothers until the age of two. Here in the Oudtshoorn facility mothers and babies are housed separately under the watchful eye of social worker Natalie Petersen.

NATALIE PETERSEN
SOCIAL WORKER At this moment we make preference for a baby to be here with their mother incarcerated within the ages from 0 to 2 years. The reason why I think that was chosen because to establish the bond between a newly born baby and their mother so that they would be able to recognise their mother some years after the mother's release as well.
V/O For Cursha growing up under the care of her parents, life in the township of Bongolethu was never easy.
DIANA LOURENS
CURSHA’S MOTHER

I only wanted the best for her. It is not that I neglected my other two children but I just wanted the best for her. Whenever she put a foot wrong I attacked her with my fists or anything else I could lay my hands on. Maybe that was the reason that she drifted away and started using that tik.
Ek wou maar net die beste vir haar gehad het, Dis nie dat ek my ander twee kinders eenkant toe geskuif het nie, maar vir haar wil ek net die beste gehad het. En as sy ‘n voet verkeerd gesit het, het ek met vuiste haar bygekom. Of enige ding wat ek in my hande kry het ek haar bygekom. Miskien het ek ook dit aangehelp omdat sy weggedryf het of daai tik gaan opsoek het.
V/O
DEREK
At the age of 16 Cursha fell pregnant with her first child, left school and was eventually arrested for dealing drugs.
DIANA LOURENS
My heart was broken because no parent wants to see her child in such a place.

I would say so yes. It gave me peace of mind when she was in prison, because in prison she is safe. There are no drugs there, there is no alcohol.
There they learn about the Lord. My hart was stukkend want geen ouer wil haar kind in so plek sien nie.

DEREK: Do you feel she was actually safer in prison?

Ek sal so se ja, Dit was vir my meer ‘n gemoedsrus dat sy in die tronk was, want in die tronk is sy veilig. Daar is nie drugs nie, daar is nie alcohol nie. Daar leer hulle van die Here.
CURSHA JANSEN

I think its better for parents here.
Out there you struggle. Here you don’t do drugs and strange things.
The outside world is very dangerous. Dink ek dit beter af vir vir ouers hier binne,
Daar buite moet jy sukkel.

Hier doen jy nie drugs en snaakse dinge nie.
Die buitelewe is baie gevaarlik.
V/O
DEREK
Cursha has been in the facility for almost a year now, and she will soon be released on parole and will face the daunting task of raising her children on the outside, with the support of her family.

NATALIE PETERSEN Sometimes yes, they do want to come back, especially when it comes to their support system. You will find some of our offenders they do not have family anymore. And one of them maybe moved to a nearby town to be with a boyfriend. Now they were abused by him and it happened that she assaulted him and now I don't wanna go back to this circumstances. But how do I face my family? What we do also, we create the opportunity to reintegrate with their families and to re-establish any communication with the family.
SHARMAINE TYA TYA They feel in here they get things that they don’t get outside. Outside you must go out, you’ve been in prison, you’ve got a criminal record. Who’s going to employ you? You don’t get a job, you don’t have a place to stay. You family don’t want to accept you. So where do you go? Back to the family in prison.
LINK
DEREK ON CAMERA These women may be safe here but it comes at the price of freedom. It's 3'oClock in the afternoon and they'll be behind bars for the next 15 hours until daybreak.

JOHANN vd WESTHUIZEN It is not a place where anybody would like to be. If its really better for you inside than outside at home with your family then its say something very negative about our society and about the levels of poverty and the social breakdown of our society.

NATALIE PETERSEN This is not a place where you can spend the rest of your life. You have to at some time learn how to be a community member. So we encourage them a lot of times to get involved in community service, to learn to give back to your community so that it brings back the feeling of I am here I belong here.
